title: Lowest Calorie Alcohol: Drinks Ranked by Calories and Carbs
excerpt: The lowest calorie alcoholic drinks ranked, from spirits with soda to light beer, hard seltzer, and dry wine, plus the best options if you're trying to lose weight.
metaDescription: The lowest calorie alcohol ranked: spirits, light beer, hard seltzer, and wine by calories and carbs, plus the best picks if you're trying to lose weight.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the lowest calorie alcoholic drinks are a single shot of straight spirits (vodka, gin, tequila, rum, or whiskey) with a zero-calorie mixer like soda water or diet tonic, at roughly 95 to 100 calories each. Close behind are ultra-light beers (about 55 to 100 calories a can), hard seltzers (about 90 to 100 calories a can), and a small glass of dry wine or brut sparkling wine (about 90 to 125 calories). The drinks that quietly blow up a calorie budget are the sweet ones: regular tonic, cola, juice, syrups, cream liqueurs, frozen cocktails, and big craft beers.

**The quick rules:** Most of the calories in any drink come from two places, the alcohol itself and the sugar added to it. Alcohol carries about 7 calories per gram, so you can't make a strong drink "zero calorie," but you can strip out almost all of the sugar. Pick lower-proof drinks, smaller pours, and mixers with no sugar. And remember that the number of drinks matters far more than which drink you choose: three light beers still beat six vodka sodas.

> **A note on health and safety.** This guide is about choosing lighter drinks if you already drink. It is not a reason to drink more, and no alcoholic drink is a health food. If you are pregnant, take medications that interact with alcohol, have diabetes, or have been told to avoid alcohol, follow your doctor's advice over anything here. Diet mixers can make you feel the alcohol faster (more on that below), so lighter drinks still call for a plan to get home safely.

## Lowest Calorie Alcohol at a Glance: The Ranked List

Here are the common drinks ranked from lightest to heaviest per typical serving. Calories are approximate. They vary by brand, recipe, and pour size, so check the label or the brand's nutrition page when it matters to you.

| Rank | Drink (typical serving) | Approx. calories | Approx. carbs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ultra-low ABV light beer, 12 oz (around 2.4 to 2.8% ABV) | 55 to 65 | 2 to 3 g |
| 2 | Brut or extra brut sparkling wine, 4 oz flute | 85 to 95 | 1 to 2 g |
| 3 | 80-proof spirit + soda water, 1.5 oz shot | about 97 | 0 g |
| 4 | Light beer, 12 oz (around 4 to 4.2% ABV) | 95 to 110 | 3 to 7 g |
| 5 | Hard seltzer, 12 oz (5% ABV) | 90 to 100 | 1 to 3 g |
| 6 | Dry white or red wine, 5 oz glass | 115 to 125 | 3 to 4 g |
| 7 | Regular lager, 12 oz | 140 to 160 | 10 to 14 g |
| 8 | Gin and regular tonic | 180 to 200 | 15 to 20 g |
| 9 | IPA or craft double IPA, 12 oz | 200 to 300+ | 15 to 25 g |
| 10 | Margarita, piña colada, or other sweet cocktails | 200 to 500+ | 20 to 60+ g |

A few things stand out. The lightest beers win on calories per can because they contain less alcohol, not because of some special brewing trick. Spirits with soda water tie with light beer because a standard shot holds about the same amount of alcohol as a light beer. And sweet cocktails sit in their own league because the mixers often add more calories than the alcohol does.

## Why Alcohol Has Calories at All

Pure alcohol (ethanol) provides about 7 calories per gram. That's almost as much as fat (9 per gram) and nearly twice as much as sugar or protein (4 per gram). In the US, a "standard drink" contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol, according to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA). Multiply those two numbers and you get roughly 98 calories from the alcohol alone in every standard drink, before any sugar, malt, or mixer is counted.

That single fact explains most of the ranked list:

- **A 1.5 oz shot of 80-proof spirits** is one standard drink and has about 97 calories, almost all from alcohol.
- **A 12 oz light beer at about 4.2% ABV** is a bit under one standard drink, plus a few grams of leftover carbohydrate, so it lands near 100.
- **A 5 oz glass of 12% wine** is one standard drink plus a few grams of residual sugar, so it lands a little higher, around 120.
- **A 12 oz IPA at 7% ABV** is closer to one and a half standard drinks, plus more malt sugars, so it can pass 200.

The practical takeaway: **the strength of a drink sets its calorie floor.** A higher-proof spirit (say a 100-proof bourbon) or a higher-ABV beer will always carry more calories per serving than a lighter version, even with nothing added. You can lower calories by choosing lower-ABV drinks or smaller pours, and you can lower them by cutting sugar. Those are the only two levers.

## Spirits: Usually the Lightest Base

Plain distilled spirits contain essentially no carbohydrate, fat, or protein. Their calories come almost entirely from alcohol, which is why vodka, gin, tequila, rum, and whiskey at the same proof have nearly identical calorie counts. Vodka isn't "lighter" than whiskey at the same strength. The differences people notice come from proof and from what goes in the glass with them.

| Spirit, 1.5 oz | Proof | Approx. calories |
|---|---|---|
| Vodka, gin, rum, tequila, whiskey | 80 | about 97 |
| Same spirits | 86 | about 105 |
| Same spirits | 90 | about 110 |
| Same spirits | 100 | about 124 |

Flavored and "infused" spirits are the exception. Many flavored vodkas are still zero sugar, but some flavored whiskeys, spiced rums, and anything labeled "liqueur" or "cream" contain added sugar, sometimes a lot. Liqueurs like triple sec, amaretto, coffee liqueur, and Irish cream can run well over 100 calories per 1.5 oz before you add anything else.

### Which spirit is best for a low-calorie night?

On calories alone, any 80-proof clear or aged spirit is a tie. If you're choosing between them, two other factors are worth considering:

- **Congeners.** Darker spirits like bourbon, brandy, and dark rum contain more congeners, by-products of fermentation and aging. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues (published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010) found that bourbon produced somewhat worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. Clear spirits won't spare you a hangover, but they may be slightly gentler. Our pages on [vodka hangovers](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and [tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) go deeper.
- **How you drink it.** A spirit you enjoy sipping neat or on the rocks will usually be drunk more slowly than one you need to mask with a sweet mixer, and slower drinking tends to mean fewer drinks overall.

## Mixers: Where Most Hidden Calories Live

The mixer can easily double or triple the calories in a highball. A 12 oz can of regular cola has about 140 calories. Regular tonic water surprises people: it's sweetened, at roughly 120 to 130 calories per 12 oz. Orange and cranberry juice cocktails are similar or higher. Ginger beer is often sweeter than cola.

| Mixer (about 6 oz, a typical highball pour) | Approx. calories |
|---|---|
| Soda water, seltzer, sparkling mineral water | 0 |
| Diet tonic, diet cola, zero-sugar ginger ale | 0 to 5 |
| Fresh lime or lemon juice (0.5 oz) | about 5 to 10 |
| Regular tonic water | 60 to 65 |
| Regular cola | about 70 |
| Orange juice | about 80 |
| Cranberry juice cocktail | about 80 to 90 |
| Ginger beer | 60 to 90 |
| Simple syrup (1 oz) | about 50 to 70 |

### The lowest calorie mixed drinks

These keep close to the calorie floor of the spirit itself:

- **Vodka soda with lime** (about 100 calories). The classic for a reason.
- **Tequila soda (a "ranch water" with lime and sparkling mineral water)** (about 100 to 105 calories).
- **Gin and diet tonic** (about 100 calories), versus 180 or more with regular tonic.
- **Whiskey highball** with soda water (about 100 calories).
- **Rum and diet cola** (about 100 calories).
- **Spritz made with soda water instead of extra prosecco**, or a wine spritzer (half wine, half soda) at about 60 to 70 calories for a 5 oz glass.

### A safety caveat about diet mixers

There's a trade-off worth knowing. Sugar in a mixer slows how quickly alcohol leaves your stomach. A 2013 study by Marczinski and Stamates in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* found that people who drank vodka with a diet mixer reached a noticeably higher breath alcohol concentration than people who drank the same vodka with a sugar-sweetened mixer. The participants didn't feel more drunk, but they were.

In plain terms: a vodka and diet soda saves you calories but may hit harder and faster than you expect. That matters for driving (don't), for pacing, and for anyone who drinks on an empty stomach to "save" calories. Eat a real meal, count your drinks rather than going by how you feel, and alternate with water.

## Beer: Light Beer and Ultra-Light Options

Beer calories come from both alcohol and the carbohydrates left over after brewing. A standard lager sits around 140 to 160 calories per 12 oz. Light beers cut both, usually by brewing to a slightly lower ABV and fermenting out more of the sugar.

| Beer style, 12 oz | Typical ABV | Approx. calories |
|---|---|---|
| Ultra-low ABV light beers | 2.4 to 2.8% | 55 to 65 |
| Light beer | 4.0 to 4.2% | 95 to 110 |
| "Ultra" low-carb light lagers | about 4.2% | about 95 |
| Regular American lager | about 5% | 140 to 155 |
| Stout (dry, like a classic Irish stout) | about 4.2% | about 125 |
| Pale ale | 5 to 5.5% | 160 to 180 |
| IPA | 6 to 7% | 180 to 240 |
| Double IPA, imperial stout, pastry stout | 8 to 12% | 250 to 350+ |
| Non-alcoholic beer | under 0.5% | 50 to 90 (some under 30) |

Two surprises in that table. First, a dry stout is often lighter than people assume, because its dark color comes from roasted grain, not extra sugar or alcohol. Second, craft beer is where calories climb fastest. A 16 oz pour of a 9% double IPA can easily match a small meal.

Brand calorie counts change and differ between countries, so we've kept this to ranges. If you have a regular brand, look up its current nutrition label. Most major US brewers publish them. For how beer itself affects the morning after, see our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover).

### Is light beer actually a good choice?

For calories per drink, yes. Light beer and ultra-light beer are among the lightest choices on the shelf. The catch is volume. Light beer is easy to drink quickly and in quantity, and six light beers is still around 600 calories plus about six drinks' worth of alcohol. If light beer helps you have the same number of drinks with fewer calories, great. If it means you drink more, the advantage disappears.

## Hard Seltzer: Lighter, but Not Magic

Hard seltzer is basically a light beer's calorie count dressed up as sparkling water. A standard 12 oz, 5% ABV hard seltzer is about 90 to 100 calories with 1 to 3 grams of carbs and usually little to no sugar. Most of those calories are alcohol.

Things to watch:

- **Higher-ABV versions.** "Surge," "extra," or 8% seltzers carry proportionally more calories, often 150 or more per can.
- **Tall cans.** A 19.2 oz or 24 oz can is really one and a half to two servings.
- **Ease of drinking.** Seltzers taste light, so many people drink them faster. Our page on [why hard seltzer hangovers happen](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains how that catches people out.

## Wine: Pick Dry, Watch the Pour

Wine calories come from alcohol plus any residual sugar, the grape sugar that wasn't fermented. Dry wines have very little residual sugar; sweet and dessert wines have a lot.

| Wine, 5 oz glass unless noted | Approx. calories |
|---|---|
| Brut nature or extra brut sparkling (4 oz flute) | 80 to 90 |
| Brut champagne, cava, or prosecco (4 oz flute) | 85 to 100 |
| Dry white (sauvignon blanc, pinot grigio, albariño) | 115 to 120 |
| Dry rosé | about 120 |
| Light red (pinot noir, gamay) | about 120 |
| Full-bodied red (cabernet, zinfandel, shiraz at 14 to 15% ABV) | 125 to 150 |
| Off-dry white (some rieslings, moscato) | 120 to 140+ |
| Port or dessert wine (3 oz) | 140 to 165 |

### The two wine variables that matter most

1. **Alcohol percentage.** A 15% zinfandel has about 25% more alcohol than a 12% sauvignon blanc, and calories follow. If you want a lighter wine, look for 11 to 12.5% ABV on the label. Vinho verde, many German rieslings labeled *trocken* (dry), and some sparkling wines sit at the lower end.
2. **Pour size.** A "standard" glass is 5 oz, but a generous restaurant or home pour is often 6 to 9 oz. A big pour of red can be 200 calories on its own.

On the sparkling side, labels follow a sweetness scale. From driest to sweetest: brut nature, extra brut, brut, extra dry, dry, demi-sec. Yes, "extra dry" is sweeter than "brut," which trips up nearly everyone.

If red wine tends to give you headaches, that's a separate issue from calories. Our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) covers the likely causes.

## The Highest Calorie Drinks to Watch

These are the drinks most likely to add a few hundred calories without you noticing:

- **Frozen and blended cocktails.** Piña coladas, frozen margaritas, and daiquiris made from mixes often run 300 to 500 calories or more in a restaurant-sized glass because of cream of coconut, mixes, and syrups.
- **Long Island iced tea.** Four or five spirits plus sour mix and cola. High in both alcohol and calories.
- **Cream and coffee drinks.** White Russians, mudslides, eggnog, and Irish coffee with whipped cream.
- **Mixed-drink "buckets" and pitchers.** Hard to count, easy to overdo.
- **Big craft beers.** As above, a 16 oz imperial stout can pass 400 calories.
- **Ready-to-drink cocktails.** Some canned cocktails are light; many are sweetened like soda. Check the label.

### How to order a lighter version

You don't have to give up cocktails to keep calories down. A few easy swaps:

- **Margarita:** ask for tequila, fresh lime, a splash of orange liqueur or agave, and soda water, instead of a pre-made sour mix. This "skinny" style can come in around 150 to 180 calories rather than 250 or more.
- **Mojito:** less sugar or syrup, more mint and lime, topped with soda.
- **Moscow mule:** vodka, lime, and diet ginger beer.
- **Aperol or Campari spritz:** more soda water, less of the sweetened liqueur and prosecco.
- **Bloody Mary:** fairly light already, around 120 to 150 calories, because tomato juice isn't very sweet. Watch the garnishes.

## Best Alcohol for Weight Loss: What Actually Matters

People searching for "the best alcohol for weight loss" usually want a single drink that won't affect their progress. The honest answer is that there isn't one. Every alcoholic drink works against weight loss in a few ways, and the drink choice matters less than the amount.

### How alcohol affects fat loss

- **Your body burns alcohol first.** Alcohol can't be stored, so your body prioritizes clearing it. While it does, it burns less fat. A small study by Siler and colleagues (published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* in 1999) found that whole-body fat burning dropped sharply for several hours after people drank alcohol. The calories from food eaten alongside are more likely to be stored as a result.
- **It increases appetite.** Researchers have repeatedly found that drinking before or with a meal tends to increase how much people eat, sometimes called the "aperitif effect." Late-night food after drinking adds up fast.
- **It lowers your guard.** Even when you plan to eat well, alcohol makes salty, fatty food more tempting and portion control harder.
- **It disrupts sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep but tends to fragment sleep later in the night. Poor sleep is linked to more hunger and cravings the next day.
- **The next day often costs calories too.** A hangover makes a greasy breakfast, a skipped workout, and a sugary drink more likely.

### A realistic approach if you're trying to lose weight

1. **Set a number before you start.** Deciding on one or two drinks ahead of time works better than deciding in the moment.
2. **Choose drinks from the top of the ranked list.** Spirit with soda, light beer, hard seltzer, or a small glass of dry wine.
3. **Alternate with water or sparkling water.** It slows your pace and helps with hydration.
4. **Eat a proper meal first.** Protein and fiber help keep the appetite effect in check, and food slows alcohol absorption.
5. **Count the drink in your daily total.** Most calorie-tracking apps include common drinks. The NIAAA's *Rethinking Drinking* site also has a free calorie calculator for alcoholic drinks.
6. **Have drink-free days.** Fewer drinking days is usually the biggest single win.

For the fuller picture of how alcohol interacts with metabolism, see our [guide to alcohol and weight loss](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025).

## Low-Carb and Keto Drinks

If you're counting carbs rather than calories, the list looks slightly different:

- **Zero carbs:** straight spirits (vodka, gin, tequila, rum, whiskey) and spirits with soda water or a zero-sugar mixer.
- **Very low carbs (1 to 3 g):** most hard seltzers, brut nature and extra brut sparkling wines, and "ultra" low-carb light beers.
- **Low carbs (3 to 5 g):** dry wines in a standard 5 oz pour.
- **Higher carbs:** regular beer (10 to 15 g or more), sweet wines, liqueurs, and anything with juice, soda, or syrup.

Keep in mind that being low in carbs doesn't make alcohol "free" on a ketogenic diet. Your body still processes alcohol first, and many people find their tolerance drops while in ketosis, so a usual number of drinks can feel stronger. Our article on [alcohol and ketosis](/never-hungover/alcohol-ketogenic-diet-ketosis-impact-analysis-2025) covers this in more detail.

If you have diabetes, alcohol can lower blood sugar for many hours after drinking, especially if you take insulin or certain diabetes medicines. That's a medical question to go over with your doctor, not something a low-carb drink solves. Our [alcohol and blood sugar guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) explains the risks.

## Lower-Calorie Drinking Also Tends to Mean Better Mornings

Some of the same choices that cut calories also make the next day easier. That's not because calories cause hangovers. It's because the habits overlap:

- **Fewer, smaller drinks** mean less alcohol, which is the single biggest driver of hangover severity.
- **Clear spirits with soda** have fewer congeners than dark spirits and sweet liqueurs.
- **Sparkling water between drinks** slows your pace and reduces dehydration-related symptoms like headache and thirst.
- **Skipping sugary mixers** avoids the blood sugar swings that can add to next-day fatigue, though the evidence on this is limited.

Mixing drinks isn't the issue some people think. The old ["beer before liquor" rule](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) doesn't hold up; total alcohol is what counts. For more practical steps, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover). If you notice puffiness the morning after, our page on [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) explains why it happens.

## Calorie Comparison for a Typical Night Out

To show how much choices add up, here's a rough comparison of three different four-drink evenings:

| Evening | Drinks | Approx. total calories |
|---|---|---|
| Lighter | 4 vodka sodas with lime | about 400 |
| Middle | 2 light beers + 2 glasses dry white wine | about 440 |
| Heavier | 2 IPAs + 2 margaritas from mix | about 900 to 1,000 |

The "heavier" evening is more than double the "lighter" one for the same number of drinks. But notice that even the lightest version is still around 400 calories, which for many people is a fifth of the day's needs. Cutting from four drinks to two saves more than any swap.

## Reading Labels and Spotting Marketing Tricks

Alcohol labeling rules differ by country, and in the US, nutrition facts on alcohol are still largely voluntary. A few things to keep in mind:

- **"Light" and "low-carb" are relative.** A "light" craft beer might still be 130 calories. Check the number.
- **"Skinny" and "clean" are marketing words.** They don't have a fixed definition on alcohol labels. Look for calories and ABV.
- **Serving size matters.** Some cans are 16, 19.2, or 24 oz. Calories on the front may be "per 12 oz."
- **"Zero sugar" doesn't mean zero calories.** The alcohol still counts, at about 7 calories per gram.
- **Restaurant pours aren't standard.** A glass of wine or a cocktail out can be much bigger than the standard serving the calorie counts are based on.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people who choose lighter drinks are also trying to make the next day easier. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's popular as a hangover supplement. Animal and lab studies suggest it may affect how the body processes alcohol and may support the liver, but human evidence is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM helps with weight loss, cuts the calories in a drink, or lets you drink more safely.

If you want to try it for the morning after, popular options include the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. It works best as one part of a sensible plan: fewer drinks, lighter drinks, food, and water.

## The Bottom Line

The lowest calorie alcohol is a single shot of 80-proof spirit with soda water or a zero-sugar mixer, at about 100 calories. Ultra-light beers, light beers, hard seltzers, brut sparkling wine, and small glasses of dry wine come close behind. Sugar-heavy cocktails, regular tonic, juice mixers, liqueurs, and big craft beers are where calories climb. If weight loss is the goal, the number of drinks and the food that comes with them matter far more than which bottle you pick.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the lowest calorie alcoholic drink?**

A 1.5 oz shot of 80-proof spirit (vodka, gin, tequila, rum, or whiskey) with soda water or a zero-sugar mixer is about 97 to 100 calories. Ultra-low-alcohol light beers (around 2.4 to 2.8% ABV) can be even lower at about 55 to 65 calories per 12 oz can. Brut sparkling wine in a 4 oz flute is around 85 to 100 calories.

**What is the best alcohol for weight loss?**

No alcoholic drink helps with weight loss, and all of them slow fat burning while your body clears the alcohol. If you're going to drink while trying to lose weight, the least disruptive choices are spirits with soda water, light beer, hard seltzer, or a small glass of dry wine, kept to one or two drinks. The number of drinks and the late-night food that often follows matter more than the type of drink.

**Is vodka lower in calories than whiskey or tequila?**

Not at the same proof. Plain 80-proof vodka, gin, tequila, rum, and whiskey all contain roughly 97 calories per 1.5 oz shot, because almost all of their calories come from the alcohol. Calories rise with proof (a 100-proof spirit is about 124 calories per shot) and with sweet mixers or flavorings.

**Are hard seltzers lower in calories than beer?**

They're lower than regular beer and similar to light beer. A 12 oz, 5% hard seltzer is about 90 to 100 calories with 1 to 3 grams of carbs, compared with about 140 to 155 for a regular lager and about 95 to 110 for a light beer. Higher-strength and tall-can seltzers carry more calories.

**Which wine has the fewest calories?**

Dry wines with lower alcohol have the fewest. Brut nature, extra brut, and brut sparkling wines are lightest at about 80 to 100 calories per 4 oz flute. Among still wines, a dry white or light red at 11 to 12.5% ABV is around 115 to 120 calories per 5 oz glass. High-alcohol reds and sweet or dessert wines are higher.

**What alcohol has zero carbs?**

Plain distilled spirits, such as vodka, gin, tequila, rum, and whiskey, have essentially zero carbs. They still have calories from alcohol, about 97 per 1.5 oz shot at 80 proof. Flavored spirits and liqueurs can contain added sugar, so check the label.

**Is it bad to mix alcohol with diet soda?**

It saves calories, but there's a trade-off. A 2013 study found that people who drank vodka with a diet mixer reached a higher breath alcohol level than those who drank it with a sugared mixer, without feeling more drunk. Count your drinks, eat beforehand, and never drive after drinking regardless of how you feel.

**Does low-calorie alcohol cause less of a hangover?**

Not directly. Hangovers depend mostly on how much alcohol you drink. That said, some lower-calorie habits help: fewer drinks, clear spirits that contain fewer congeners than dark spirits, and sparkling water between drinks. There is no good evidence that any low-calorie drink or supplement prevents a hangover if you drink heavily.
